about.title: Oakland Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: When a hospital stay or clinic visit in Oakland leaves you worse off than when you arrived, the first question is usually a quiet one: was that supposed to happen? Sometimes the honest answer is yes. Medicine carries risk, and a poor result by itself is not malpractice under California law. Other times a provider fell below the standard of care that a reasonably careful doctor, nurse, or pharmacist would have met, and that gap caused real harm. Sorting one from the other takes records, time, and a qualified medical expert, which California almost always requires before a claim can move forward. Oakland is home to more than 419,000 people served by a dense mix of hospitals, urgent-care centers, and specialty practices across Alameda County, so these questions come up here regularly. Our team handles medical negligence claims locally and works on contingency, meaning no fee unless your case produces a recovery.

items.title: MICRA deadlines are short and layered
items.desc: California generally gives one year from when you discovered the injury, and never more than three years from the injury itself, plus a 90-day notice must go to the provider before suit. We can map those dates against your own records.

items.title: An expert is nearly always required
items.desc: Under California law, a qualified medical expert must typically confirm that care fell below the accepted standard. Our team knows how to line up that review early rather than late.

items.title: The non-economic cap changes yearly
items.desc: MICRA limits non-economic damages such as pain and suffering, and that cap rises each year by statute. Knowing which figure applies to your timeline matters, and we can explain it plainly.

items.question: Where would an Oakland medical malpractice lawsuit actually be filed?
items.answer: Claims arising from care in Oakland are generally filed in Alameda County Superior Court. Before any filing, California requires a 90-day notice of intent to the provider. Our team handles that notice and the court process; you focus on your health.

items.question: My surgery went badly. Does that mean I have a case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. A bad outcome alone is not malpractice in California; the question is whether the provider did something a reasonably careful provider would not have done, and whether that caused your harm. A qualified medical expert is almost always needed to answer that, which is why an early records review is so useful.

items.question: How long do I have to act after a medical error in California?
items.answer: Generally one year from the date you discovered, or should have discovered, the injury, and no more than three years from the injury itself. There are narrow exceptions, but waiting to find out is risky. Contact us for a free conversation about your specific dates.
